title: How bullying led Britain's Campbell to the UFC
description: Introduced to combat sports as a seven-year-old after being bullied at school, Kurtis Campbell is now chasing success in the UFC.
fullText:
Kurtis Campbell was only seven years old when his parents decided something drastically needed to change.

During his time at primary school in Liverpool, Campbell was targeted by bullies. His parents, Jay and Michelle, could see the effect it was having.

It was then that they signed him up for Muay Thai classes to help him learn how to defend himself.

"From there, I've never looked back," Briton Campbell told BBC Sport. "I've been in love with the sport ever since."

Without his parents' influence and support, the 24-year-old would not be chasing his dream of becoming a UFC champion.

Seventeen years later Campbell is preparing for his second fight in the promotion against American Trevor Peek at UFC Paris on Saturday.

"I'm not going to stop until my mum and dad are on a beach somewhere, sipping cocktails and doing nothing else for the rest of their lives," Campbell said.

"They can enjoy it, knowing that they've created this monster. That's my plan."

Initially, it seemed Campbell's time in the gym would serve the sole purpose of learning self-defence before moving to secondary school a couple of years later.

That was until he started competing in amateur competitions, slowly but surely becoming obsessed with his newfound escape from the difficulties he faced at school.

"I was quite a soft kid, in the sense that I didn't really like the violence or the fighting," Campbell said.

"I felt like when I did fight, and when I really did go into it, everything changed and I never looked back."

Aged 15, he won his first international Muay Thai title and started to realise that, with the blessing of his parents, combat sports could become more than just a pastime.

"I was never the cleverest kid. I was always in the bottom sets at school, so I wasn't really focused," Campbell said.

"All of the teachers told me, 'you need to do something else. You have to have a plan B.'"

But for Campbell, who was beginning to attract attention across Merseyside, his unwavering commitment to the sport meant there was no need for a back-up plan.

That included regularly running almost five miles to and from school. There was even one occasion when he missed school while studying for his GCSEs to attend a coaching seminar in Liverpool hosted by John Kavanagh - the coach of former two-weight UFC champion Conor McGregor.

After completing his GCSE exams at the age of 16, Campbell enrolled on a college course that combined studying for a qualification in sport with playing football.

Or at least that was what he was supposed to be doing.

Campbell struck an arrangement with the course leads that allowed him to attend classes before leaving to train in combat sports, while his peers were on the football pitch.

"I was always avoiding anything just for fighting," Campbell said.

"I really didn't like school. It wasn't me. But I made a good few mates there, so you've got to take the pros with the cons."

When Campbell suffered a TKO defeat by Danny Silva on his UFC debut in March, it was the first time in almost seven and a half years that he had lost.

Not since December 2018, when he lost to fellow Liverpudlian Liam McCracken on the local amateur circuit, had featherweight Campbell failed to get his hand raised.

He won five titles across three different weight classes with the Full Contact Contender (FCC) promotion before earning a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series in September 2025.

It means that when he steps into the Accor Arena to fight Peek, he will face the unfamiliar feeling of trying to bounce back from defeat.

"Fighting in the UFC was just the goal and the dream when I was younger," Campbell said.

"So I feel like that fat kid looking back at me would be proud of me. I would be proud of myself, no matter how the debut went, just because of where I am now.

"I think he'd be happy with me. But I know he'd not be happy with just the story. I've still got a lot of legacy to build.

"That's one thing I would say is good and bad about me - as soon as I get something, I want more of it.

"I don't think I'll ever stop having that feeling."

title: Former world champion Ruiz Jr loses comeback fight
description: American heavyweight Andy Ruiz Jr, who shocked Anthony Joshua in 2019 to take his world titles, loses comeback fight to Poland's Damian Knyba.
fullText:
Former world champion Andy Ruiz Jr has vowed to carry on after losing his comeback fight to Poland's Damian Knyba in New Jersey.

The 36-year-old heavyweight shocked the boxing world seven years ago by beating Britain's Anthony Joshua to take his world titles.

Ruiz Jr has since been beset by injuries and was taking part in just his fourth fight since losing the rematch to Joshua in December 2019.

He looked a shadow of his former self at the Prudential Center in Newark, saved by the bell after scrambling back to his feet following a knockdown in the seventh, he eventually lost by a unanimous points decision.

Judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in favour of the Pole, who took his record to 18 wins and one defeat, but Ruiz Jr was quick to demand a rematch.

"I don't know, I think it was just him holding," said Ruiz Jr, who recently signed up with British promoter Eddie Hearn.

"Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

"He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different."

Joshua's former conqueror argued that he was simply rusty after taking his first fight since drawing with American Jarrell Miller in August 2024.

"It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent," he argued.

"I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again."

title: Exclusive-White House reviews candidates to replace Hegseth deputy Feinberg, sources say
description: , Erin Banco and David Jeans WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The White House has reviewed candidates to potentially replace Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, three
fullText:
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The White House has reviewed candidates to potentially replace Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, a sign that more leadership change could come for a Pentagon already facing unusually high staff turnover.

The effort, which was ‌under way in June, has included conversations with senior lawmakers in the Senate about whether the administration's picks would have enough support to be confirmed, said two of ‌the people, one of whom added that the review was still going on as of late August. Reuters could not determine when the White House began considering candidates.

The three sources said no decision had been made to remove Feinberg from his ​post. They did not say why the White House was reviewing potential replacements and did not specify which candidates the White House was considering.

"These so-called anonymous 'sources' have no idea what they are talking about," said White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly.

"President Trump appreciates the work of Secretary Hegseth, Deputy Secretary Feinberg, and the entire Department of War, whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself," she said, referring to U.S. military operations in Iran and Venezuela.

The Pentagon denied a process was under way to replace Feinberg. Asked for comment by Reuters, Hegseth said in a ‌statement that Feinberg has his full support and "isn't going anywhere."

The Pentagon ⁠did not provide a comment from Feinberg and declined to make him available for an interview.

A departure by Feinberg, the billionaire co-founder of private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management, would be the most senior staff change for a department that has already seen a string of high-profile departures under Secretary of Defense ⁠Pete Hegseth.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week following months of tension with Hegseth, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Army has declined to comment on the reasons for his departure. Navy Secretary John Phelan and several senior Army leaders have also departed in recent months.

Feinberg, who vowed to accelerate U.S. munitions production, has not yet met that goal, according to analysts who say that the U.S. industrial base ​cannot ​ramp up quickly. Some defense industry executives say his task has been complicated by the slow pace of Congress ​appropriating funds despite immense pressure from the administration.

Feinberg "has worked tirelessly to rebuild our ‌Defense Industrial Base and ensure our military has everything it needs to win, and I look forward to continuing to work with him," Hegseth said in his statement to Reuters, adding, "He's doing a tremendous job for President Trump, for the Department, and for our warfighters."

Trump has increasingly expressed frustration with the lack of progress in the six-month-old Iran war, which has settled into a costly standoff between the U.S. and Iran.

One of the costs has been a drawdown of U.S. weapons stockpiles. Reuters has reported that the U.S. military faces significant shortages of certain munitions, which have alarmed Congress and military leaders.

Trump has dismissed the concerns, saying the U.S. has "far more munitions than anyone in the world."

But in an exchange with Trump at Camp David earlier this month, ‌according to the Washington Post, Hegseth blamed Feinberg for letting stockpiles of long-range guided missiles and air-defense interceptors shrink.

The ​White House has called the report "fake news." In a statement to Reuters, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said: "Secretary Hegseth did ​not mislead anyone about our munitions posture, and he did not blame Deputy Secretary Feinberg."

Appointed ​by Trump last year, Feinberg has attempted to reshape the Pentagon by ramping up the U.S. military's direct investments in companies and delivering loans to military ‌contractors through multiple offices inside the department, including the Office of Strategic ​Capital and the newly created Economic Defense Unit.

In an ​August 18 memo he sent to defense firms and seen by Reuters, Feinberg called on contractors to speed up production and provide more transparency around pricing. The Pentagon did not respond to a question about the memo.

Feinberg has also come under scrutiny on Capitol Hill, where Democratic U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren has raised concerns about whether his former firm Cerberus ​could benefit from the Pentagon's spending on its Golden Dome missile ‌defense program.

"There are no conflicts of interest between Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg and Cerberus," said Parnell. "He has completely divested from Cerberus and has recused himself from ​any conversations or business relationships between the Executive Branch and Cerberus."

Cerberus did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Opinion - Russia starved, tortured a US Marine for 4 years — stop treating Putin like an ally
description: Some of conservative media’s loudest voices insist Russia is a friend. But look at what the Russians did to one of our countrymen.
fullText:
Russia finally released ailing former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman after 1,666 days in captivity. The man who came home was a shadow of his former self: emaciated, frail, and denied proper medical care for the entirety of his imprisonment.

That is the condition an American citizen was in when Vladimir Putin's regime handed him back on what it called a "humanitarian basis."

Gilman was so starved during his years in Russian custody that, according to President Trump, the one thing he asked for when he got on the plane home was a cheeseburger. It is shocking to think that one of the "few and the proud," held for more than four years by a country some of conservative media's loudest voices insist is a friend, came out of custody asking for a basic meal.

Sadly, Gilman's is not an isolated case. At least 10 Americans have been confirmed by our own government to be held under harsh conditions against their will in Russia. Five of them — Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian and Chuck Zimmerman — have been identified by advocates as meeting the U.S. government's own criteria for wrongful detention. Every one of them is reported to be facing serious medical concerns like the ones that nearly killed Gilman.

What kind of country jails American citizens, starves them, withholds basic health care and then expects us to smile and pretend everything is fine when one is returned?

That is precisely what a loud faction on the right keeps asking us to do.

Prominent voices, including Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson among them, have spent years telling their audiences that Russia is a traditional, high-functioning Christian society with admirable values and world-class health care. In May, Owens traveled to sanctioned Russia to speak at a state-sponsored conference. She came home praising the wonders of the Russian health care system.

Russian healthcare is so great that they just sent an American Marine home catatonic, starving, and riddled with pneumonia after denying him medical care for years.

I heard what Russian captivity does to people firsthand when I interviewed Ukrainian prisoners of war who had survived Russian custody. They described systematic beatings, starvation and daily torture. The first thing they had to do in custody was come to understand that a human being could be treated this way by another person. It is heartbreaking, but over 95 percent of Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85 percent of captured civilians are tortured or mistreated by Russia, according to the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

That is why a group of Ukrainian prisoners of war recently pleaded their case before an informal gathering of the United Nations Security Council. Russia's deputy U.N. Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya responded to their testimony by calling it "a disinformation campaign against Russia."

I have heard the stories directly from former Ukrainian prisoners of war. Ukraine's military intelligence agency showed me pictures of a Ukrainian prisoner who had been cut open, without anesthesia, for a surgical procedure, leaving behind a massive scar across his belly and a "Z" — the symbol of Russian invaders — that looked like it was burned into his skin. He was practically branded like cattle.

A Ukrainian plastic surgeon has since removed the "Z" free of charge so the man didn't have to live with a constant reminder of the torture he endured while in Russian captivity.

Will American media voices keep entertaining the fiction that Vladimir Putin is a man we can trust, while American citizens are still being held hostage in Russia? The plane that brought Gilman home should have been filled with every remaining American in Russian custody. Putin does not become a good man, let alone someone the U.S. government should thank, simply because he released one American his own military had tortured.

I'm not calling for war or abandoning diplomacy. I am asking Americans to wake up. Putin's Russia is not America's ally. It is an adversary that brutalizes our citizens and counts on our commentators to explain it away, along with Russia's own state sponsored media organs that push propaganda all day long.

The right thing — the America First thing — is to bring every American home who is still in Russian captivity, and to understand that Russia is deliberately depriving Americans of their liberty and torturing them, just as it has done to thousands of Ukrainians throughout the course of this war.

Laura Loomer is an investigative journalist and the founder of Loomered.com. She recently reported from Ukraine, where she interviewed Ukrainian prisoners of war released from Russian captivity, and President Volodymyr Zelensky.

title: Man Utd made midfield recruitment summer priority - what happens now?
description: Michael Carrick says Manchester United have balance in their midfield following a £150m summer recruitment campaign - so who plays?
fullText:
Michael Carrick struck a chord with many Manchester United fans as he lavished praise on Kobbie Mainoo after his side's thrilling 5-2 victory over Ipswich at Old Trafford, calling the midfielder's performance "immense".

Starting in the Premier League for the first time since he surprisingly failed to play a minute at the World Cup, Mainoo caught the eye with his performance and Carrick made sure the 21-year-old was not overlooked on a day skipper Bruno Fernandes scored a hat-trick.

But former United goalkeeper Ben Foster had a different take.

"I love Kobbie," Foster wrote on his Threads account.

"He's the future, but he's not there yet. Be honest with yourself and you'll know he's not gonna be one of the first four or five names on the team sheet.

"If he can get a year out on loan where he is the main man, where he is needed and relied upon every single game, that will instil something in him he won't get at Manchester United."

The social media reaction suggested Foster had got it wrong.

There are plenty of people who feel Mainoo absolutely should be one of the "first four or five names" in Carrick's side.

But, if that was correct, what would it mean for the three international midfielders United have spent more than £150m on this summer after identifying it as a priority area?

Carrick is about to feel the impact of United's qualification for the Champions League.

Last season, United had two midweek games in the second half of the season. They drew at West Ham and lost at Newcastle. They then had 13 and 11-day gaps to their next fixture respectively.

Starting with their trip to Everton, United have five games in 16 days before the first international break of the campaign.

If Carrick's side progress in the EFL Cup, they won't have a spare midweek until Christmas.

Rotation is inevitable in United's new-look midfield this season - but what will that look like?

In assessing the signings that have been made, Carrick speaks about balance.

Brazil midfielder Casemiro left at the end of his contract while Uruguyan Manuel Ugarte - likely to leave anyway had he not suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury during the World Cup - is out until next year.

That left Mainoo, Bruno Fernandes and Mason Mount as United's only senior central midfielders going into the summer transfer window, with the latter pair better suited to more advanced roles.

After missing out on Elliott Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, United moved quickly to sign Brazilian Andrey Santos from Chelsea for £48m. A day later, Belgium's 29-year-old Youri Tielemans joined from Aston Villa for £35m.

Santos, 22, dovetailed well with Mount during the early pre-season games, sitting deep and screening the back four.

Mount played in the number eight role and seemed to be a viable option to stay there into the new campaign until an ill-timed injury at the beginning of August provided a reminder of his unhappy record of absences.

Tielemans' pre-season appearances seemed to be based around developing an understanding with skipper Fernandes.

"Andrey, for such a young man, to come in the way has, with his character and his personality is a dream," Carrick explained when he spoke to reporters during his side's training camp in County Kildare.

"He's so positive, so mature, so switched on; he wants to learn. He comes in and straight away he's trying to help other players, talk in games and communicate. He's got a real substance to him.

"Youri's a little bit more obvious, probably because we've seen an awful lot of him and we all know him, but again, the character, the personality, the presence, and the quality on top.

"The two midfielders in particular, will give us an awful lot moving forward."

Into that mix has come Carlos Baleba.

At £70m, the Cameroon international is in the top 10 of United's most expensive signings of all time. It is the kind of fee, in the club's new era of restraint, that suggests he should also be one of the "first four or five names on the team sheet".

Each player adds something different to United's midfield.

Baleba provides speed, aggression and defensive awareness.

Tielemans has comfort on the ball, plus his passing and vision.

Santos excels in one-to-one duels. He also has defensive awareness, a good passing range and used short bursts to break defensive lines.

Mainoo's ability comes through his willingness to take the ball in tight spaces and progress it up the field.

It is a formidable array of qualities but they cannot all play at the same time.

"You sound like you're in our coaches' office trying to pick the team," said Carrick, when the general plusses and minuses of the situation were put to him before his side's trip to Everton on Sunday.

"We're not just putting a squad together for one game on Sunday. We need a squad that's going to take us through the whole season.

"There's a whole picture in there that we need to balance. Sometimes it's to change during the game, sometimes it's game-to-game, sometimes you play every three or four days.

"Whoever plays in there, we are talking about adding to the squad and feeling we've got different partnerships and combinations we can rely on to get us through a season with unfortunate injuries or suspensions or whatever may come."

title: Williams sisters exit US Open but excite - what does future hold?
description: Serena and Venus Williams may have lost in their US Open doubles return, but the veteran pair proved they can still compete on an entertaining night in New York.
fullText:
Rarely has a women's doubles first-round match headlined the US Open night session - but the Williams sisters are like no other pairing.

Serena and Venus Williams might have a combined age of 90, but their star remains undimmed. As does their ability to compete at the highest level when they are in tandem.

Even though the superstar siblings - aged 44 and 46 - lost on their highly anticipated Grand Slam return, their performance in a narrow defeat by 14th seeds Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint led to an entertaining night in New York.

A packed Arthur Ashe Stadium roared on the American icons as they looked on course for a memorable win - but ultimately fell short in a 6-3 6-7 (6-8) 7-6 (10-7) loss.

"It was unbelievable how competitive that was," said American player-turned-commentator Chanda Rubin, who lost to the Williams sisters in the 1999 US Open doubles final.

"After the first set you wondered if Serena and Venus would be able to find their mojo - but, boy, they did."

Four years after they last appeared on Ashe, the Williams sisters were given a rapturous reception as they strode on to a court where they have won eight singles titles between them and two doubles titles together.

The decibel levels were rarely matched in an underwhelming first set for the home favourites, but the noise quickly returned when they rallied in the second.

The atmosphere became muted as the decider seemed to run away from them at 4-1 down, before they showed indomitable spirit - a hallmark of their extraordinary careers - to take their opponents into a first-to-10 match tie-break.

Racing into a 5-0 lead put the Williams sisters firmly on course to reach the second round, only for Chan and Joint to fight back, with the help of a double fault from each opponent.

Despite the initial despondency of the home fans the volume was turned back up when the American pair were given a fond farewell, with everyone left wondering what the future holds for them both.

Serena hinted she wanted to play singles again in an interview with Good Morning America, external earlier this week, while Venus said after her singles exit on Monday that she should not "have to" think about her future beyond the doubles.

The questions about what happens next were not addressed by the pair following Friday's match. The sisters decided they were "not available" to speak to the media, US Open organisers said.

For once, the 20,000-odd fans on a packed Arthur Ashe Stadium sat quietly engrossed during points.

The sight of the Williams sisters back on court together at the US Open - possibly for the final time - commanded ultimate respect from a chatty crowd known to let their attention wander.

The siblings changed the face of the sport when they emerged as precocious teenagers in the 1990s, going on to dominate the sport with a combined 30 Grand Slam singles titles and 14 doubles victories as a pair.

Three decades later, the sport remains captivated by them.

Serena, a 23-time Grand Slam women's singles champion, coming out of retirement this summer sparked excitement among those who saw her in their prime and those too young to have witnessed it.

Seven-time major winner Venus has never "evolved away" from the sport - the words chosen by her younger sister when she last played in 2022 - but instead continued her career with the help of sporadic wildcards.

While that has proved controversial in some quarters, there were few objections about the sisters being invited to play once again at Flushing Meadows.

Their planned return at Wimbledon was scuppered by the knee injury which Serena suffered in her singles match there - ironically a defeat by 20-year-old Joint - before they finally reunited at the WTA event in Cincinnati.

The comeback ended in a match tie-break defeat by Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk and her American partner Peyton Stearns, with the same fate befalling them in New York.

When the Williams sisters last played on Ashe four years ago, they suffered a straight-set defeat by Czech pair Lucie Hradecka and Linda Noskova in the first round.

It looked like being a similar outcome as they meekly surrendered the first set against Chan and Joint, then batted off four break points in the fifth and seventh games of the second set.

But once Serena upped her level to match her impressive sister, they managed to switch the momentum back in their favour and level the match.

An absorbing contest featuring some sensational points saw the Americans fight back again in the decider, only to falter from a commanding lead in the tie-break.

Overall it was a more than credible performance from the veteran pair. Their solid groundstrokes, sharp movement and never-say-die attitude caused problems for their opponents, who deserve huge credit for staying focused in a partisan environment.

"The atmosphere was surreal," said Joint.

"It was something we've never experienced before, and to play against such legends of the game was super special."

title: I've never spoken to Everton owner Friedkin - Moyes
description: Everton manager David Moyes says he has never met or spoken to the club's owner Dan Friedkin.
fullText:
David Moyes says he has never met or spoken to Everton owner Dan Friedkin since returning as manager in January 2025.

Friedkin is head of The Friedkin Group, which runs the club from its base in Houston, but has not attended a home game since completing a takeover of the club in December 2024.

How the club is run and who is responsible for making key decisions came under close scrutiny during the summer transfer window.

Speaking to reporters before Everton's match against Manchester United on Sunday, Moyes reiterated his commitment to the club despite a chaotic end to the window.

When asked if he had ever met or spoken to Friedkin in the 20 months since he was reappointed as manager, Moyes' answer was a simple "No".

Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.

"My real contact is Angus," said Moyes. "Angus is the one who I would go to see. Rishi is the next one and then the head of the Friedkin family in America.

"I don't really get any direct conversations with them, but I do through Rishi, he is the one I would speak to."

Fans reacted angrily during last Saturday's match at Bournemouth following news the club had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19s midfielder Harrison Armstrong.

Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remain frustrated by decisions made by the board in the remainder of the transfer window.

Beto was sold to Fiorentina on deadline day on Tuesday, before the club had secured a replacement striker, with USA forward Folarin Balogun then backing out of a move to Everton from Monaco at the 11th hour on Tuesday.

Everton finished the transfer window with a squad of just 18 senior players, including only one striker, one right-back and one left-back.

Moyes aligned himself with Everton fans last weekend when asked about plans to sell Armstrong, saying the club was "managed by an Evertonian" and "supporters aren't always wrong".

And he acknowledged on Friday that there was work to do done on the club's structure behind the scenes: "We've got new owners in who are still feeling their way in the club. I think if we get to know each other more it will get better."

But the former Manchester United and West Ham boss said he would not walk away from the challenge of unifying a club that he led to a succession of top-five finishes in the Premier League between 2002 and 2013 in his first stint as manager.

"Everton's different," said Moyes, when asked if he had considered quitting. "I wouldn't have come back for anybody but Everton.

"I think the club here has had enough days where the people find a way of recovering. People saw the face of Evertonians last week and it can be really powerful. I would expect them to be really powerful now.

"But powerful for the team, powerful for the players. What we're going to need from them is extra because we're short, so we need them. If they're not with us, then it's terrible. And they are with us, I believe they are with us."

title: Antonelli 'disrupting rules of fandom' in Ferrari's Italy
description: BBC Sport heads to Monza to find out if Italians want Kimi Antonelli to win the F1 title or if it is all about Ferrari.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli has been hailed as a generational talent in Formula 1; the driver who can end the 73-year wait for an Italian world champion.

In March, Antonelli became the youngest-ever championship leader when he sealed victory in Japan at 19 years, seven months and four days.

And he has stayed there ever since.

This weekend, Antonelli arrives at the Italian Grand Prix with a 59-point advantage at the top of the standings after winning six races so far this year.

There is just one small issue: the young star drives for Mercedes, not Italy's beloved Ferrari.

"Ferrari is my heart," says Thomas, who is Monza born and bred, to BBC Sport at the circuit on Friday.

"It's a religion," says Emanuele, who is at the grand prix with his daughter, Matilde. "In Italy, we do support other teams and other sports, but there is only one Ferrari."

Ferrari is Formula 1 in Italy; natives joke that the position of Scuderia team principal is just as important as the identity of the Pope.

So, with fans flocking to worship at the Temple of Speed, just how do Italians feel about Antonelli battling Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc for race wins and the drivers' championship?

When a Ferrari driver triumphs in F1, the team's spiritual home of Maranello rejoices.

"It's like the second coming effectively; everyone's in the streets singing, dancing, church bells are ringing. It's a party in the streets," says Adrian Hussain, who is a member of the Scuderia Ferrari Club Silverstone and half-Italian.

Those famous bells last rung out in honour of a Ferrari world champion in 2007, when Finn Kimi Raikkonen won his only title by a single point.

Italy has not produced a world champion driver since Alberto Ascari claimed back-to-back titles for Ferrari in 1952 and 1953. For most Italians, seeing a title winner draped in il Tricolore - for any team on the grid - has been a dream rather than a reality.

But Antonelli's ascendancy this year has opened the door for Italy to embrace a new hero - even if he does drive for the direct competition.

"Antonelli is disrupting the traditional rules of fandom in Italy," Giulia Toninelli, a journalist for La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy's most widely read sports newspaper, tells BBC Sport.

Toninelli says Antonelli's "strong personality" has won over the Italian public, especially the younger fanbase. "And the fact that he is racing for Mercedes matters very little to them."

In the fanzone at Monza, a household is divided. While Alessandro is decked out in Ferrari red, his girlfriend, Emma, is wearing the silver of Mercedes.

"Of course, I am a little bit of a Ferrarista because I'm Italian. But honestly, I love Kimi, I support him," says Emma.

If Antonelli does win this year's world title, with the season finale possibly being held at Imola, about 25 miles from where he grew up in Bologna, both Emma and Alessandro agree it would mean "Italy is back on top".

Five-time MotoGP race winner Marco Melandri and 2012 GP2 series champion and F1 TV's Davide Valsecchi present the Chiacchiere da Box, external (Paddock Chatter) podcast, where the two ex-racers discuss and analyse everything that's happened during F1 and MotoGP weekends.

"I think Kimi is living the dream, even of the Italian fans," says Italian Melandri. "But in Italy, a lot of people are very close to Ferrari, they are pushing for Ferrari. So sometimes they are fighting themselves to understand, to choose who is their favourite driver. But I think Kimi is doing something amazing."

Compatriot Valsecchi feels the same: "We are loving it. It's a big surprise for everyone, knowing that an Italian driver, so young, is leading the championship, is driving so well, and is mentally so strong. So, at the moment, everything is perfect for us."

Antonelli has been a Mercedes protege since he was 11 years old.

After just one season in Formula 2, Silver Arrows team principal Toto Wolff fast-tracked him into the seat vacated by seven-time world champion Hamilton in 2025, after the Briton left to join Ferrari in a blockbuster move.

Antonelli's introduction to F1 last year was a steep learning curve, and after a bruising European leg of the season that featured four retirements and only three points, he finished his debut campaign seventh in the championship.

Mercedes have made sure to put an arm around Antonelli whenever there has been a mishap. When the then 18-year-old crashed during his very first practice session in Monza two years ago, Wolff was straight on the team radio with five soothing words: "All good, Kimi. All good."

"I think Kimi is in the right place at the moment," says Toninelli. "Mercedes is a family he has known for a long time, one that has nurtured him as a driver and given him a level of protection that would be impossible for him to have at Ferrari right now."

Being separated from the sometimes "extreme" Italian fanbase can only work in Antonelli's favour, believes Valsecchi.

"Sometimes in Italy, we lack a bit of patience," he says. "We just push for you when you are strong and then underline with red pen every time as soon as you make little mistakes.

"For this reason, as a rookie, it is better to be away and to be on another side, and then come to Ferrari only when you are a big man with already a championship and a complete driver."

If Antonelli does clinch his maiden title this year, he will surpass four-time winner Sebastian Vettel as the youngest driver in Formula 1 history to become world champion.

German Vettel was 23 years and 134 days old when he claimed his first title in 2010. Antonelli would be three years younger.

If that happens, Daniele, who is enjoying Monza with his two sons, Tommaso and Demis, says they will feel "so-so" about Antonelli's victory.

"We support Hamilton and Leclerc - we support Ferrari," says Daniele emphatically, although youngest son Demis, while still loyal to the Scuderia, is an Antonelli fan, whispering the Mercedes driver is "really good".

"I'm happy for Kimi, of course. But I'm not supporting him like Ferrari, because Ferrari is up there," Thomas adds, gesturing high into the air.

Antonelli has already rewritten the history books this season, becoming the youngest driver to take pole position, converting it into his first victory in China in March, before becoming the youngest driver to win the prestigious Monaco Grand Prix.

An engine-related retirement in Barcelona and a 15th-placed finish at Silverstone have been the only real blips of Antonelli's campaign, up until Monza's grid penalty as a result of taking a new power unit, which means he will start at the back in Sunday's race.

While his title lead has ebbed and flowed in recent races, a victory in Belgium, plus podiums in Hungary and Zandvoort, has given Antonelli a decent buffer to Mercedes team-mate George Russell and Hamilton, who are both level on 183 points.

"It would be very nice to have an Italian driver in Italian colours winning races and championships," says Hussain. "Everybody within the club, certainly in our group chats, everyone's supportive of Kimi winning races. There's no animosity towards him."

Melandri, too, thinks Antonelli driving the red car could happen somewhere along the line. "It should be a dream to see Antonelli get a victory in Ferrari in the future. That's for sure," he adds.

At the drivers' news conference at the Belgian Grand Prix in July, after Antonelli had been hanging out with tennis' five-time Grand Slam champion and compatriot Jannik Sinner, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson asked Antonelli who, out of the two of them, is more famous in Italy.

His light-hearted reply was rapid. "It's Charles," he said, pointing to Ferrari's Leclerc sat next to him. "He's probably the most famous man in Italy right now."

Monegasque Leclerc has become the surrogate son of the Scuderia since his arrival in 2019, carrying the hopes of the tifosi on his shoulders for the past eight seasons.

Fluent in Italian and deeply embedded in Ferrari's culture, the 28-year-old, who has won twice at Monza, signed a new long-term deal with the team in June, and has said his desire to be the driver that delivers success back to Maranello is what fuels his title ambitions.

But with just nine wins for the team in 162 grands prix, doubts as to whether Leclerc is truly the chosen one for Ferrari might be starting to creep in.

"I start to see, after many years, for the first time, some fans start to say, maybe he's not as strong as we think before, because Hamilton is doing better than him, and Antonelli is doing much better with another car," says Melandri.

With Antonelli hamstrung by his grid drop this weekend, Ferrari have a head start on their rival. If he does manage to recover and finish in the top three, would a Scuderia one-two accompanied by some Antonelli magic be the ideal race result?

"Of course, sharing the podium with a Ferrari would make it even more special, but regardless of that, he will have the full support of his fans," says Toninelli.

"Part of the Italian audience may indeed favour Ferrari over Kimi, while another section may feel the opposite, but that won't stop the Italian celebration at Monza, which will bring both fanbases together."

title: 24 hours that show how preoccupied Trump is
description: It can be difficult to decide which Roman metaphor more aptly captures President Donald Trump’s posture these days.
fullText:
It can be difficult to decide which Roman metaphor more aptly captures President Donald Trump's posture these days.

Is it "bread and circuses," feeding the American people a series of distractions — amusing or otherwise — from their worries about the economy? Or is it Nero, fiddling with his ballroom plans while the Republican Party's midterm hopes burn?

What's clear is that Trump and his administration aren't going to course correct any time soon.

The last 24 hours have been a case in point. And the last couple weeks have been inauspicious for anyone who hoped Trump might suddenly focus on the political task at hand.

Thursday marked exactly two months until Election Day 2026. And the first votes are about to be cast, with North Carolina sending out mail ballots on Friday.

But despite a bevy of polling showing Americans want Trump to focus on affordability and the economy, he appears preoccupied with anything but.

On Thursday alone, we learned the Trump administration has hired a new pool contractor to clean up the mess he made of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, announced the start of construction on Trump's 250-foot "triumphal arch" and launched a series of arcade-style video games, including one that allows users to arrest undocumented immigrants.

The White House is also reportedly launching a reality show-like competition for entrepreneurs, just weeks after Trump's "Patriot Games" flopped and after an actual reality show from the Department of Transportation was released. (It says a nonprofit paid for it; not taxpayers.)

Trump even sat for an interview — and gave a construction tour, of course — for the New York Magazine piece.

Reporter Ben Terris reported that the president's official calendar is "peppered with meetings about other projects around Washington that can often last an hour or longer."

And in perhaps the most eyebrow-raising scene, Trump actually agrees with Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's contention that he's building monuments to himself because he doesn't think others can be counted on to do it.

"That's true," Trump said. "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will."

The fact that Trump would say this out loud is stunning. Ossoff meant this as a dig.

But it also suggests Trump might be feeling the pressure to get these projects done fast. He has a finite amount of time to plaster his name on things and build things that he'll be remembered by. It could get more difficult by January, when Democrats could control one or both chambers of Congress.

Trump even talks about how it will supposedly be impossible for Democrats to demolish his ballroom, if they wanted to. ("It's nuclear concrete," he told New York Magazine. "I think it would be very hard. It's meant for if there's a nuclear attack.")

Terris also runs through how Trump in his public appearances often seems distracted by his construction projects as he's attending to much more serious business.

And that's really the problem with all of this, at least if you're a congressional Republican staring at a concerning midterm election.

It's not just that Trump is distracted; it's that he's focused on things that polls show Americans view as frivolous and don't want — at the expense of things they really want him to do (i.e. lowering prices and ending the war with Iran).

Trump's ballroom is 2-to-1 unpopular.

Americans opposed his 250-foot "triumphal arch" 52%-21% in an April poll.

A July poll showed 65% of Americans described themselves as upset or dissatisfied with the ballroom, arch and Reflecting Pool projects.

While Trump tries to put his name on things like the Kennedy Center, just 9% of Americans think that's appropriate for him to do as an incumbent president.

And Trump's other preoccupation in recent days and weeks — his new trade war with Canada, which led him move to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" — fares little better. Reuters-Ipsos polling this week showed Americans opposed the Canada tariffs 57%-20% and the "Lake America" renaming 63%-14%.

Trump last week held a White House event for the latter move, which it turns out even his fellow Republicans oppose by double digits.

All of this cements a tough picture for the GOP. Polling has for months shown that Americans view Trump as neglecting more important fare.

CBS News polling has recently shown 78% of Americans said he's not focused enough on lowering prices, and July CNN polling shows around the same percentage (73%) said he hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems.

It's not fair to say Trump has completely neglected the cost of living.

He recently announced he would pause tariffs on imported beef to try to lower prices for consumers, and on Friday he threatened to stop trading with other countries if the Federal Reserve doesn't lower interest rates.

Both moves could theoretically save people money.

But both moves also betray Trump's preference for questionable quick fixes. The beef tariffs move, for example, is expected to have a negligible impact, CNN reported, while irritating domestic cattle ranchers and even some Republicans. And the extortionate threat to the Fed seems unlikely to bear fruit. (Indeed, lowering interest rates could actually send inflation higher.)

The CNN poll in July contained another telling finding. Fully 66% of Americans said Trump did not put the good of the country above his own personal gain. That included 76% of independents and 30% of Republicans.

And more than a month later, with the 2026 general election truly kicking off, it's as if he's bent on proving those people right.

title: Non-citizen police officers approved after Dem says ICE 'invasion' 'sends a message'
description: Danbury, Connecticut's city council voted 18-2 to let non-citizen immigrants and DACA recipients serve as police officers amid ongoing ICE raids.
fullText:
After a week of ICE raids, the Democrat-dominated City Council of Danbury, Connecticut, voted nearly unanimously to approve non-citizen legal residents serving as police officers.

Under the new guidance, approved in an 18-2 vote, non-citizen legal residents and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients living in Danbury are allowed to serve as police officers in Danbury.

One city council member, Democrat Joe Britton, remarked that the vote "sends a message to our immigrant community at large that you are welcome in Danbury."

ICE operations in the area resulted in more than 60 arrests, according to local reports. The arrests prompted public outrage in the community, including from city officials such as Britton, who called the raids "frightening."

Border Czar Tom Homan Fires Back After Democrat Chris Murphy Claims Ice Is 'Terrorizing Little Kids'

The only two council members to vote against the measure were Republicans, while the council's 17 Democrats and one Republican voted in favor.

Before the vote, Britton said that "what we have here is an opportunity." He noted that "though this definitely wasn't planned to be on the agenda on the end of a federal invasion of immigration officials in Danbury … I do think it's timely."

"There is no reason to vote against this, and if you do vote against this, I truly question your moral compass," he added.

Britton emphasized that this change "is legal, it's allowed" and said it has been recommended.

Britton told Fox News Digital that "Danbury is an immigrant city, and I believe someone who is lawfully here, committed to our community, and willing to raise their hand and take an oath to protect and serve should have the opportunity to do so."

He added that "this change does not lower Danbury's standards for becoming a police officer. It simply allows otherwise qualified lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply and compete for these positions."

He noted that "every applicant must still satisfy the same training, background, character, and certification requirements required of any other officer," saying, "This was about expanding the pool of qualified applicants while maintaining the same high standards our residents expect from their police department."

Similarly, Taylor O'Brien, a spokesperson for the Danbury city government, told Fox News Digital that council "amended its ordinance in accordance with Connecticut's Police Officer Standards and Training Council, allowing legal permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply to become officers in the Danbury Police Department."

Dem Senate Nominee Changes Tune On Ice After Vowing Not 'One More Dime' For Agency

O'Brien said that "this standard is followed by over 30 municipalities in Connecticut and several states across the country" and that it "opens Danbury's applicant pool to otherwise qualified candidates, including legal Danbury residents, who are currently applying to be police officers in other communities."

In 2020, the Connecticut Police Officer Standards and Training Council "partially waived" the citizenship requirement, extending eligibility for law enforcement candidates in Connecticut to lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients, according to the Connecticut Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection.

O'Brien added that Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, a Democrat, "ensures Danbury maintains a rigorous hiring process for our Police Officers," adding that "this amendment should encourage qualified residents from the Danbury community to apply to serve the City they call home."

According to the Danbury News Times, Alves himself immigrated to the U.S. as an "undocumented child" and gained citizenship in 2017.

The outlet quoted Alves saying he is "glad the City Council approved" the measure. Alves emphasized that "the standards are not being lowered" and that "every applicant still has to meet the same rigorous background, training, fitness and professional standards required of any Danbury police officer."

"What we are doing is giving qualified people an opportunity to compete for the job," said Alves. "For a diverse city like Danbury, it strengthens our recruitment pool and gives us another opportunity to hire talented people who understand and care about the community they want to serve."

Fox News Digital reached out to Britton for additional comment.

Last year, ICE arrested two illegal immigrants who were serving as police officers. On July 25, 2025, Jamaican national Jon Luke Evans, who was serving as a reserve officer with the Old Orchard Beach, Maine, Police Department, was arrested on charges related to unlawfully attempting to purchase a gun. Then, on Oct. 15, Radule Bojovic, of Montenegro, who was serving as a police officer with the Hanover Park, Illinois, Police Department, was arrested during Operation Midway Blitz.

Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

title: A US Army commander says facing Ukrainian hunters helped his troops figure out how to use armor in a drone-heavy fight
description: Russia's war in Ukraine has demonstrated that tanks and armored vehicles are vulnerable to drone threats. Obsolescence, though, is up for debate.
fullText:
A US Army commander wrote an op-ed about his troops' recent training fight against Ukrainian forces.

While drones were a problem, he said soldiers adapted their techniques, especially with their armored vehicles.

Officials and experts have debated the vulnerability of armored vehicles against drones.

A US Army commander wrote in a new opinion article that a recent combat training exercise against Ukrainian soldiers showed that armor like infantry fighting vehicles and tanks can still survive and make a difference on battlefields swarming with drones, but troops have to be able to adapt, to flexibly change how they move, hide, and fight.

During the simulated battle, his troops saw how persistent drone surveillance exposed their movements and put their combat vehicles at risk. But the soldiers also learned and adapted, the commander said.

On Friday, Capt. Allan W. Watson, the commander of Blackhawk Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment, wrote an op-ed in Task and Purpose about an April exercise. The exercise, held at Hohenfels Training Area in Germany, pit Watson's soldiers against Hohenfels' dedicated opposition force, the 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, with support from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Force's 412 Regiment.

The Ukrainian unit, known as "Nemesis," brought real combat experience fighting with and against drones to the training, presenting a demanding test for American soldiers. Reconnaissance drones tracked their movements, and US forces didn't have the counter-drone capabilities they wanted, Watson wrote.

Watson's soldiers responded by changing how they used their armored vehicles. They hid their Bradleys in gullies and among the trees, leveraged the terrain to mask their maneuvers, avoided predictable routes that they knew the Ukrainian hunters expected them to try, and deliberately considered how the force looked to overhead drones.

"More than once," he wrote, "I found myself standing sideways in the turret of our Bradley, barking orders as our platoons traversed 40-degree slopes, finding new routes to an objective."

"The enemy still found us," Watson wrote in the op-ed. But "even with drone reconnaissance, the enemy had to use traditional ground reconnaissance and infiltration techniques. While a drone could identify us from above, only troops on the ground could exploit the information."

Throughout the fight, the US forces lost Bradleys and tanks, which Watson said was expected in a high-pressure event like this, an exercise meant to resemble a real armed conflict.

For Watson, those losses didn't condemn his armored assets to irrelevance; rather, the training exercise demonstrated that armor still provides tremendously valuable mobility, protection, and firepower as long as it is put to use with the drone threat in mind.

"Our armor did not make us more vulnerable," he wrote, "it made us mobile, protected, and dangerous."

Officials and top war watchers have debated the value of armored vehicles against drones and uncrewed systems since the beginning of the Ukraine war, as reports from the front and video footage of drones blowing up tanks and armor across the battlefield circulated online.

The asymmetric threat raised concerns that the proliferation of cheap drones, both surveillance and attack, had made heavy armor too vulnerable, making it less relevant for future fights.

Watson's account of his experiences paints a more complicated picture, acknowledging that uncrewed systems represent a growing threat to armored combat vehicles but emphasizing that the threat hasn't yet made them obsolete. The debate goes on.

title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
description:
A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.
These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.

fullText:
A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models

Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.

These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.

Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.

That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.

Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.

“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”

The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.

There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.

He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.

Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.

Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.

Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.

The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.

With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.

AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.

Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.

Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.

The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.

OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.

The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.

OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.

“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”

His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”

And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.

He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

title: Iranian tanker hit by US attack near Iran's Kharg Island, Tasnim says
description: DUBAI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - An Iranian tanker was hit by U.S. forces on Saturday near Iran's key oil export hub, Kharg Island, in the Gulf, the semi-official Iranian news agency Tasnim reported.
fullText:
DUBAI, Sept 5 (Reuters) - An Iranian tanker was hit by U.S. forces on Saturday near Iran's key oil export hub, ‌Kharg Island, in the Gulf, the semi-official Iranian news agency Tasnim ‌reported.

According to a Tasnim correspondent from Kharg, the tanker was hit by four U.S. ​missiles in the area of Kharg Island's anchorage.

Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker's crew was being evacuated.

There was no immediate official announcement by Iranian authorities and U.S. Central Command did ‌not immediately respond to ⁠a request for comment.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on August 31 in a one-line social media post accompanied by ⁠an AI-generated video that Kharg Island was being "blown to smithereens". Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.

Iran is the third-largest ​producer in ​the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting ​Countries and exported 90% of ‌its crude via Kharg Island before the war, but flows have been disrupted since a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.

Trump said on June 11 that he wanted to take over Kharg Island, but then said a threatened U.S. military operation there was off the ‌table for now, days before Tehran ​and Washington signed an interim agreement aimed ​at ending the war on ​June 17.

A U.S. attack on Kharg would heap further ‌pressure on Iran's oil industry and ​its wider economy, ​which is already reeling from the U.S. naval blockade.

The U.S. imposed its blockade on Iranian ports after Iran effectively shut the Strait ​of Hormuz, a key ‌waterway that carried one-fifth of the world's oil supply before ​the war.

title: Russia’s Sechin says China, not OPEC, calls shots on global energy markets
description: VLADIVOSTOK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Igor Sechin, chief of Russia’s top oil producer Rosneft, said on Thursday that China, not OPEC, has stabilized global oil markets by reducing crude imports by 5.5
fullText:
VLADIVOSTOK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Igor Sechin, chief of Russia's top oil producer Rosneft, said ‌on Thursday that China, not OPEC, has ‌stabilized global oil markets by reducing crude imports by 5.5 ​million barrels per day this year.

Sechin, the most influential Russian energy manager and a long-standing ally of President Vladimir Putin, was speaking at a ‌Russian - Chinese business ⁠forum in the far eastern city of Vladivostok.

"This year, China has effectively ⁠taken the lead from OPEC and, without being a member of any cartel, has managed to ​stabilise the ​global oil market by ​cutting its oil ‌imports by 5.5 million barrels per day," Sechin said.

Sechin, known for his skepticism towards OPEC, said China will get more influence on the energy markets as the number of OPEC members is ‌declining.

"I believe that further growth ​in China's reserves will ​strengthen China's role ​in the energy market, against a ‌backdrop of OPEC's waning influence ​and a ​reduction in the number of its members," Sechin said.

Earlier this year, the United Arab Emirates ​declared its ‌withdrawal from the group.

title: Rock concert at Virginia's Wolf Trap canceled after worker is crushed to death beneath tour bus
description: A tour bus support apparatus failed at Wolf Trap National Park, crushing a worker underneath, hours before Squeeze was set to perform Thursday.
fullText:
A rock performance at a venue in Virginia was canceled Thursday after a man working on a tour bus in a nearby parking lot was crushed underneath it hours before the show, according to authorities.

U.S. Park Police told Fox 5 Dc they responded to the Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts at 5 p.m.

The English rock band "Squeeze" was scheduled to perform at 7:30 p.m. that night.

The worker was under the tour bus when officers arrived. Park Police said a supporting apparatus failed, causing the bus to come down on him.

Connecticut Dad Jumped To His Death During Concert At Madison Square Garden In Nyc: Report

"There was an accident involving a member of the community at Wolf Trap National Park," the venue said in a social media post. "Out of respect, tonight's show has been canceled."

"Squeeze are deeply saddened and shocked by an incident that occurred at the venue earlier today, which resulted in the loss of a life," the band said in a statement to Rolling Stone. "We will work with the promoter and venue regarding the possibility of rescheduling the show and will communicate further information to ticket holders as soon as it is available. Our thoughts remain with everyone affected by this tragic event."

Country Star Mark Chesnutt's Longtime Bandmate Dies Unexpectedly On Tour Bus

The worker's identity has not been released by Park Police.

News of the accident prompted some fans to leave, but many lingered in the parking lot, shaken by the death of the worker.

"It was horrible when we found out that happened," Debbie Daniel told FOX 5 DC. "We saw the emergency vehicles come in, figured something serious had happened because there was like 15 or more vehicles. But, yeah, it was very tragic."

Eric Anderson, another fan, empathized with the man's colleagues and agreed with the decision to cancel the show.

title: Pelosi, Omar join Trump and Schiff as unlikely alliance pushes to onshore key industry
description: Adam Schiff, Nancy Pelosi and Ilhan Omar back Donald Trump's federal film tax incentive to bring movie production back to California and America.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump has gained several unlikely allies, including the man who led his first impeachment trial, in a major push to bring motion picture production back to California from other countries.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., who represented studio-heavy Burbank in Congress, was joined by Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., in echoing support for Trump's federal tax incentive plan to draw major film projects back to where it began.

"We've been promoting that for a long time. I'm glad he finally arrived at it," Pelosi told Fox News Digital when asked about the plan on the Capitol grounds.

Paramount Escalates Threat To Leave California As Dem Ag's Antitrust Lawsuit Stalls Warner Bros Merger

Schiff tweeted earlier this week that he is "in strong agreement with the president."

The Democrat, who has accused Trump of colluding with Moscow to win the election and whom the president has responded to by calling him "pencil-neck," said it is time for Republicans and Democrats to "work together… get this done and bring the movie magic back to America."

Schiff Attack On Trump's Dc Indycar Race Backfires After Driver Points Out Contradiction

"Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we've lost to other countries."

Omar told Fox News Digital a similar refrain, adding that she has worked separately to attract film projects to Minneapolis.

Film Producer Says 'Made In America' Movies Can Help Revive Hollywood's Struggling Industry

She referenced "Fargo," the 1996 Coen Brothers comedy starring William H. Macy as an example of Minnesota's ability to host large projects. The "Mighty Ducks" series starring Emilio Estevez and Joshua Jackson also filmed heavily in the Twin Cities during its 1990s run.

"When I was in the Minnesota House, I was very supportive of Minnesota having subsidies so we can have more movies being made inside Minnesota like the movie 'Fargo'," she said.

She said the end of subsidies from St. Paul recently "made it less fun trying to run into people who were actually doing the production."

"It could be a really cool thing [and] also bring us money to states that can use it."

Trump appointed legendary actors Jon Voight, Mel Gibson and Sylvester Stallone special envoys to Hollywood. Gibson previously told Fox News that for a recent film, it was cheaper to fly the entire crew to Europe for three days than to shoot for one day in Los Angeles.

"There's something really wrong there," he said, adding that another actor, ex-California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, tried to assuage the problem while in office but was met with "obstacles."

Last year, another Trump foil also got on board with the idea of Washington bolstering Hollywood.

"California built the film industry – and we're ready to bring even more jobs home… Now it's time for a real federal partnership to Make America Film Again," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

What happened to Ben Simmons? Complete career timeline
description: The Sacramento Kings and Ben Simmons agree to a one-year deal. Here's a look back at Simmons' career in the NBA.
fullText:
Ben Simmons has been through a share of ups and downs throughout his NBA career since entering the league as the No. 1 pick in the 2016 draft. He's officially back in the league.

Simmons returns to an NBA roster after signing with the Sacramento Kings filling out their final open spot, a source close to the team confirmed to USA TODAY Sports. Simmons is signing a one-year, $3.5 million contract with the Kings, according to ESPN, who were first to report the signing.

Simmons has missed time throughout his career due to chronic back problems and a series of leg injuries. He took time off last year, missing the entire 2025-26 season to rehabilitate his body from his lingering injuries. He's battled through physical and mental adversity throughout his career, but now he's ready to get back on the court.

Here's a look back at what Simmons has been through in his NBA career:

Ben Simmons came into the NBA as a bonafide star, coming out of LSU where he averaged 19.2 points, 11.8 rebounds, 4.8 assists, two steals and nearly a block per game as a freshman in 2015-2016. He always has been looked at as a guy who can do a little bit of anything and everything on the floor.

Simmons went on to become the No. 1 pick the 2016 NBA Draft, selected by the Philadelphia 76ers. However, Simmons missed the entire 2016-17 season after rolling his ankle in his first practice, causing a fracture in his right foot and ankle, which did not heal throughout the season.

The following seasons, Simmons was healthy and he proved why he was worthy of a top pick. He won the NBA Rookie of the Year award in 2018 since he never technically played a game his first year, and the 76ers advanced to the NBA playoffs. He averaged 15.8 points, 8.1 rebounds, 8.2 assists, 1.7 steals and 0.9 blocks that year. The Sixers lost in the second round of the playoffs to the Boston Celtics in five games.

Simmons earned his first All-Star selection during the 2018-2019 season, and the 76ers made another postseason appearance losing to the eventual champion Toronto Raptors in a seven-game Eastern Conference semifinal series that ended in a game-winning shot from Kawhi Leonard.

Simmons continued to excel as a playmaker offensively and showcased ability on the defensive end, earning first-team All-Defense honors, along with another All-Star appearance in 2019-20, but the 76ers were swept in the first round by the Celtics.

Simmons continued to show his versatility into the following season in 2020-21, in which he was an All-Star again, an All-Defense first-team selection again and even runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year. Philadelphia lost to the Atlanta Hawks in Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals. It was the infamous game that Simmons passed up a wide open dunk or layup as Philadelphia trailed, 88-86, with 3:30 remaining. It changed his career.

Simmons asked for a trade during the 2021 offseason and caused a holdout, not appearing for training camp or preseason. He said he was away dealing with his mental health. Simmons ended up missing the entire 2021-22 with a back injury in addition to mental health hurdles from the previous postseason, along with a trade holdout from Philadelphia. He was traded to the Brooklyn Nets in February 2022.

He came back the next season but only for a limited time. Simmons played 43 games in 2022-23 dealing with a series of knee and lingering back issues. His back issues continued into the next season in 2023-24, during which he appeared in 15 games with the Nets before being shut down with continued back pain that required surgery.

Simmons played 33 games with the Nets before he was waived during the 2024-25 season. He signed with the Los Angeles Clippers in February 2025, but appeared in only 18 games as he struggled with his physical health and athletic mobility. He became a free agent after the season.

Simmons missed the entire 2025-26 season to focus on his return, completely resting to focus on his rehab.

Simmons returns to NBA, fresh and ready to hoop. The Kings believe so, as well.

Simmons gives them an additional ball handler on a roster that heralds Zach LaVine, Domantas Sabonis and the No. 7 overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, Darius Acuff Jr.

Simmons isn't coming in a stranger. He and LaVine met each other when they were young. Both Sabonis and Simmons were in the same draft class a decade ago.

Simmons is expected to function as a backup point guard to Acuff, but can see minutes alongside him as well, according to a source close to the team.

General manager Scott Perry and head coach Doug Christie have often publicly emphasized a desire to be a team that believes in playing rugged defense. Simmons' signing adds to their pillars. The Kings can benefit from his 6-foot-10, 240-pound frame. A source close to the team said there's belief in his versatility to defend every position on the floor that'll make Sacramento a bigger team.

There's optimism that Simmons' past injuries are behind him and the Kings are taking that chance.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: What happened to Ben Simmons? Complete career timeline

title: NFL's Top 100 snubbed one of the Cowboys most important players
description: The NFL unveiled their Top 100 list yet Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith was left off the rankings making it one of the biggest snubs in 2026
fullText:
The NFL's Top 100 list has been completely revealed, yet there is one glaring omission in the form of Cowboys left guard Tyler Smith.

The list is voted on by players themselves designed to recognize the league's best, making Smith's absence particularly notable as he has become one of the NFL's most dependable and feared offensive lineman.

The 25-year-old earned his third-consecutive Pro Bowl selection this past season since moving from tackle to guard in 2023.

ESPN voted Smith as the top interior lineman in their annual positional rankings yet it was not enough to earn a spot from his peers throughout the league. In total, the list named just eight total offensive lineman; five tackles, two guards, and one center.

Execs, coaches, scouts rank Top 10 interior offensive linemen: 

-ZERO consensus among 1-7
-Tyler Smith has HOF ability
-Chiefs' star tandem slips 
-Meinerz, Thuney ⬆️
-Skoronski next for big $
-Brewer one of best success stories
-Zabel a starhttps://t.co/Nzn1IjvH9T

ESPN also ranked Smith as the 88th best player on their annual Top 100 list yet that voting group is comprised of 12 analysts and reporters — not peer-driven.

Dallas also believes highly in Smith's services after they gave him a four-year, $96 million extension almost a year to the day, locking him up through the 2030 season. At the time, it made him the highest-paid guard in all of football.

This snub should give Smith and the rest of this Cowboys' line more fuel to add to the collective fire that anchors one of the best offenses in all of football.

In all, only three Dallas players made the list with wideout CeeDee Lamb coming in at No. 55, receiver George Pickens at No. 36, and quarterback Dak Prescott the highest ranked Cowboy at No. 31.

His absence from the Top 100 doesn't necessarily change his standing around the league, but it does raise questions about how the voting process values offensive lineman.
